From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Population_by_U.S._state.svg/250px-Population_by_U.S._state.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Population_by_U.S._state.svg)

Resident population of each [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state"), the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") in 2024 according to the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Census_Bureau "U.S. Census Bureau")

The [states and territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_and_territories_of_the_United_States "List of states and territories of the United States") included in the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau")'s statistics for the United States population, ethnicity, and most other categories include the [50 states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Separate statistics are maintained for the five permanently inhabited [territories of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"): [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam"), the [U.S. Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands"), [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), and the [Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-1)

As of April 1, 2020, the date of the [2020 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the nine most populous [U.S. states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") contain slightly more than half of the total population. The 25 least populous states contain less than one-sixth of the total population. [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), the most populous state, contains more people than the 21 least populous states combined, and [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"), the least populous state, has a population less than any of the 31 most populous U.S. cities. The population of Wyoming currently as of 2025 is 588,753.

## Method

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Method")]

The [United States Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census "United States Census") counts the persons residing in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") including [citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship "Citizenship"), non-citizen [permanent residents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_residence_(United_States) "Permanent residence (United States)"), and non-citizen long-term visitors.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-2) Civilian and military federal employees serving abroad and their dependents are counted in their home state.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-3)

## Electoral apportionment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Electoral apportionment")]

Every 10 years, the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") is charged with making an actual count of all residents by state and territory. The accuracy of this count is then tested after the fact, and sometimes statistically significant undercounts or overcounts occur. For example, for the [2020 decennial census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), 14 states had significant miscounts ranging from 1.5% to 6.6%. While these adjustments may be reflected in government programs over the following decade, the 10-year representative apportionments discussed below are not changed to reflect the miscount.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-4)

### House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: House of Representatives")]

Based on this decennial census, each state is allocated a portion of the 435 fixed seats in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") (until the early 20th century, the apportionment process generally increased the size of the House based on the results of the census until the size of the House was capped by the [Reapportionment Act of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reapportionment_Act_of_1929 "Reapportionment Act of 1929")), with each state guaranteed at least one Representative. The [allocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment "United States congressional apportionment") is based on each state's proportion of the combined population of the [fifty states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") (not including the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam"), [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), the [Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands"), [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), or the [U.S. Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands")).

### Electoral College

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Electoral College")]

The [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), every four years, elects the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and [Vice President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") based on the popular vote in each state and the District of Columbia. Each state's number of votes in the Electoral College is equal to its number of members in the Senate plus members in the House of Representatives.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-auto-5)

The [Twenty-third Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-third_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-third Amendment to the United States Constitution") additionally grants the District of Columbia (D.C.), which is not a state, as many Electoral College votes as it would have if it _were_ a state, while having no more votes than the least populous state (Wyoming). Since the U.S. Constitution guarantees every state at least one member of the U.S. House of Representatives and two members of the U.S. Senate, every state has at least three Electoral College votes. Thus, the Electoral College has 538 members (100 [senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), plus 435 representatives due to the limit imposed by the Reapportionment Act of 1929, plus 3 members for the District of Columbia).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-auto-5)[Territories of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States") are not included in the Electoral College: people in those territories cannot vote directly for the President of the United States,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-6) although they may participate in the partisan nominating primaries and caucuses.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-7)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Population_by_U.S._state.svg/250px-Population_by_U.S._state.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Population_by_U.S._state.svg)

Resident population of each [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state"), the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") in 2024 according to the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Census_Bureau "U.S. Census Bureau")

The [states and territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_and_territories_of_the_United_States "List of states and territories of the United States") included in the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau")'s statistics for the United States population, ethnicity, and most other categories include the [50 states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Separate statistics are maintained for the five permanently inhabited [territories of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"): [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam"), the [U.S. Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands"), [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), and the [Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-1)

As of April 1, 2020, the date of the [2020 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the nine most populous [U.S. states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") contain slightly more than half of the total population. The 25 least populous states contain less than one-sixth of the total population. [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), the most populous state, contains more people than the 21 least populous states combined, and [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"), the least populous state, has a population less than any of the 31 most populous U.S. cities. The population of Wyoming currently as of 2025 is 588,753.

## Method

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Method")]

The [United States Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census "United States Census") counts the persons residing in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") including [citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship "Citizenship"), non-citizen [permanent residents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_residence_(United_States) "Permanent residence (United States)"), and non-citizen long-term visitors.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-2) Civilian and military federal employees serving abroad and their dependents are counted in their home state.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-3)

## Electoral apportionment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Electoral apportionment")]

Every 10 years, the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") is charged with making an actual count of all residents by state and territory. The accuracy of this count is then tested after the fact, and sometimes statistically significant undercounts or overcounts occur. For example, for the [2020 decennial census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), 14 states had significant miscounts ranging from 1.5% to 6.6%. While these adjustments may be reflected in government programs over the following decade, the 10-year representative apportionments discussed below are not changed to reflect the miscount.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-4)

### House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: House of Representatives")]

Based on this decennial census, each state is allocated a portion of the 435 fixed seats in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") (until the early 20th century, the apportionment process generally increased the size of the House based on the results of the census until the size of the House was capped by the [Reapportionment Act of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reapportionment_Act_of_1929 "Reapportionment Act of 1929")), with each state guaranteed at least one Representative. The [allocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment "United States congressional apportionment") is based on each state's proportion of the combined population of the [fifty states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") (not including the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam"), [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), the [Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands"), [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), or the [U.S. Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands")).

### Electoral College

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Electoral College")]

The [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), every four years, elects the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and [Vice President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") based on the popular vote in each state and the District of Columbia. Each state's number of votes in the Electoral College is equal to its number of members in the Senate plus members in the House of Representatives.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-auto-5)

The [Twenty-third Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-third_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-third Amendment to the United States Constitution") additionally grants the District of Columbia (D.C.), which is not a state, as many Electoral College votes as it would have if it _were_ a state, while having no more votes than the least populous state (Wyoming). Since the U.S. Constitution guarantees every state at least one member of the U.S. House of Representatives and two members of the U.S. Senate, every state has at least three Electoral College votes. Thus, the Electoral College has 538 members (100 [senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), plus 435 representatives due to the limit imposed by the Reapportionment Act of 1929, plus 3 members for the District of Columbia).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-auto-5)[Territories of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States") are not included in the Electoral College: people in those territories cannot vote directly for the President of the United States,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-6) although they may participate in the partisan nominating primaries and caucuses.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-7)

Extract what this page can establish even if it cannot answer the whole question.
Preserve exact names, titles, dates, values, units and relevant lists. For tables,
keep each value attached to its entity and header, including year, variant and
population. Distinguish different measurements and totals from subgroups. Quote
short supporting text. Report missing fields as unknown. If the supplied page is
truncated, do not claim its unseen rows or candidates are absent. Describe list
coverage and date range so partial evidence cannot be mistaken for a complete set.

The current-page note is saved before navigation. Follow a page link when its label,
surrounding text or an observed same-site URL pattern suggests it can fill a
specific missing field. State that field and why the next page should supply it.
A relevant index may contain useful links without answer facts. A wrong-year page
can help if it links to the required year. Generic footer links on unrelated pages,
missing pages and repeated content do not justify expansion. After an unhelpful
child, choose a different supported route or stop. You may follow links outside
the menu and infer another address within a site already being read.

Child notes are preserved separately and returned automatically. Never rewrite
them as your own evidence. Keep useful Next links in your note even if the local
expansion budget is exhausted; unvisited links are not disqualified candidates.

**Evidence:** Relevant facts, lists or rows with exact fields and short source quotes.

**Original Question:**
Among the 20 most populated US states in 2020 according to the United States Census Bureau, which states voted in favor of the Democratic Presidential candidate with a lead of 10% or more in the U.S. Presidential Election of the same year (2020), had a teen birth rate of less than or equal to 13 per 1,000 females aged 15-19 according to the CDC Teen Birth Rate by State for the same year (2020), and had suicide mortality rates of less than or equal to 11 per 100,000 total population according to the CDC Suicide Mortality Rates by State for the same year (2020)?

**Previous Reasoning Steps:**
[turn 1] We need to find among the 20 most populated US states in 2020 (by Census, top 20) which states satisfy:

- Voted in favor of Democratic Presidential candidate with a lead of 10% or more in 2020 election (i.e., margin >= 10%).
Democratic candidate is Biden. So states where Biden won by a margin >= 10% (difference between Biden and Trump >=10 percentage points).
We need a list of states from top 20 that meet that.

- Teen birth rate <=13 per 1000 females aged 15-19 from CDC Teen Birth Rate by State 2020.

- Suicide mortality rates <=11 per 100k total population from CDC Suicide Mortality Rates by State 2020.

We need those states meeting all three.

First we need to identify the top 20 most populated states in 2020. We can get from Census data: 2020 Census population list. Top 20:

1. California
2. Texas
3. Florida
4. New York
5. Pennsylvania
6. Illinois

9. North Carolina

Let's verify with a source. Search.

[turn 2] We need to identify the states that satisfy three conditions, among the top 20 most populated U.S. states in 2020 (Census). The conditions:

1. Voted in favor of the Democratic Presidential candidate with a lead of 10% or more in 2020 election. That means that the state gave majority to Biden with margin >=10 percentage points.

2. Teen birth rate <=13 per 1,000 female 15-19 in 2020 (CDC Teen Birth Rate by State 2020). Need to source each state's rate.

3. Suicide mortality rate <=11 per 100k total population 2020 (CDC Suicide Mortality Rates by State 2020).

We need to find which states meet all three, from the top 20 most populous states. Provide answer: list of such states.

We need to use web_search and web_fetch to get data. Let's first fetch top 20 list. Wikipedia page likely lists top 20 states. Let's open it.

[turn 3] We need check each of the 20 states for:

1. voted for Democratic Presidential candidate (Biden) with a lead of 10% or more in 2020. That is margin >10% in favor of Democrats? In 2020, some states were >10% but need the list.

2. teen birth rate <=13 per 1k females 15-19 per CDC 2020.

3. suicide mortality <=11 per 100k per CDC 2020.

We need to find which states satisfy all three.

We will need to fetch data.

Let's fetch the 2020 election results by state page.

[Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election "United States presidential election") were held in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on November 3, 2020.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-ElectionDay-1) The [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") ticket of former [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States")[Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") junior [senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")[Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") defeated the incumbent [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")[president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and vice president [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-12) The election saw the highest [voter turnout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_turnout_in_United_States_presidential_elections "Voter turnout in United States presidential elections") by percentage [since 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_United_States_presidential_election "1900 United States presidential election"). Biden received more than 81 million votes,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-:7-13) the [most votes ever cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_candidates_by_number_of_votes_received "List of United States presidential candidates by number of votes received") for a presidential candidate in U.S. history.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-:8-14)

In a competitive primary that featured the most candidates for any political party in the [modern era of American politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Party_System "Sixth Party System"), Biden secured the [Democratic presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"). Biden's running mate, Harris, became the first African American, first Asian American, and third female[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-15) vice presidential nominee on a major party ticket. Trump easily secured re-nomination with only minor opposition in the [Republican primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Republican Party presidential primaries"). [Jo Jorgensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Jorgensen "Jo Jorgensen") secured the [Libertarian presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Libertarian_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Libertarian Party presidential primaries") with [Spike Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Cohen "Spike Cohen") as her running mate, and [Howie Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howie_Hawkins "Howie Hawkins") secured the [Green presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Green_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Green Party presidential primaries") with [Angela Nicole Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Nicole_Walker "Angela Nicole Walker") as his running mate.

The central issues of the election included the public health and [economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), [civil unrest in reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests "George Floyd protests") to the police [murder of George Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd"), the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") following the [death of Ruth Bader Ginsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg "Death and state funeral of Ruth Bader Ginsburg") and [confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Coney_Barrett_Supreme_Court_nomination "Amy Coney Barrett Supreme Court nomination"), and the future of the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-16) Due to the ongoing pandemic, a record number of ballots were [cast early](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_voting "Early voting") and [by mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting "Postal voting").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-:9-17) Thirty-eight states had over half of all votes cast using these methods, and only three states had fewer than 25%.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-18) As a result of a large number of mail-in ballots, some [swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state") saw delays in vote counting and reporting; this led to major news outlets delaying their projection of Biden and Harris as the [president-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_transition_of_Joe_Biden "Presidential transition of Joe Biden") and [vice president-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president-elect_of_the_United_States "Vice president-elect of the United States") until the morning of November 7, 2020.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-math-19)

Biden defeated Trump, winning 306 [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College") votes and 51.3% of the popular vote to Trump's 232 electoral votes and 46.8% of the popular vote. Trump was the first president to lose re-election since [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election"). Key to Biden's pivotal victory were his wins in the Democratic-leaning [Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt "Rust Belt") states of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Michigan "2020 United States presidential election in Michigan"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2020 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania"), and [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Wisconsin "2020 United States presidential election in Wisconsin"), which Trump narrowly carried in 2016 and whose combined 46 electoral votes were enough to swing the election to either candidate. This election marked the first time since [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_United_States_presidential_election "1948 United States presidential election") that the Democratic candidate won the popular vote in four consecutive elections.

Trump refused to accept the results; he and his allies made disproven claims of fraud, pressured election officials, filed several unsuccessful lawsuits,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-20)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-21)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-22) and directly [attempted to overturn the results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election "Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election") at the county, state, and federal level. This culminated in an [attack on the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack") on January 6, 2021, for which [Trump was impeached a second time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump "Second impeachment of Donald Trump"). The day after the attack, Trump stated that a "new administration" would be succeeding his, without mentioning president-elect Biden by name, in a video posted on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-23)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-24)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-25)

## Background

Further information: [United States presidential election §Procedure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election#Procedure "United States presidential election")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Donald_Trump_official_portrait.jpg/250px-Donald_Trump_official_portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_official_portrait.jpg)

[Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), the incumbent president in 2020, whose first non-consecutive term expired at noon on January 20, 2021

The [Maine Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Legislature "Maine Legislature") passed a bill in August 2019 adopting [ranked-choice voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranked-choice_voting_in_the_United_States "Ranked-choice voting in the United States") (RCV) both for presidential primaries and for the general election.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-ovz9x-26)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-qhJpi-27) Governor [Janet Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Mills "Janet Mills") allowed the bill to become law without her signature, which delayed its taking effect until after the [2020 Democratic primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Maine_Democratic_primary "2020 Maine Democratic primary") in March and made Maine the first state to use RCV for a presidential general election. The [Maine Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Republican_Party "Maine Republican Party") filed signatures for a [veto referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veto_referendum "Veto referendum") to preclude the use of RCV for the 2020 election, but [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Secretary_of_State "Maine Secretary of State")[Matthew Dunlap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Dunlap "Matthew Dunlap") found there were insufficient valid signatures to qualify for the ballot. A challenge in [Maine Superior Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Superior_Court "Maine Superior Court") was successful for the Maine Republican Party, but the [Maine Supreme Judicial Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Supreme_Judicial_Court "Maine Supreme Judicial Court")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-28)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-29) stayed the ruling pending appeal on September 8, 2020.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-30) Nevertheless, ballots began being printed later that day without the veto referendum and including RCV for the presidential election,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-31)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-forbes-32) and the Court ruled in favor of the secretary of state on September 22, allowing RCV to be used.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-33) An emergency appeal to the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") was denied on October 6.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-34) The law continues the use of the [congressional district method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_district_method "Congressional district method") for the allocation of Maine's electors ([Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") is the only other state that apportions its electoral votes this way).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-FcJYG-35) While multiple rounds of vote counting were not needed due to a single candidate receiving a majority of first-choice votes statewide and in each district, use of RCV complicates interpretation of the national [popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_election "Direct election") because voters are more likely to vote for third-party or independent candidates.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-36)

On December 14, 2020, pledged electors for each candidate, known collectively as the [United States Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), gathered in their states' capitols to cast their official votes. Pursuant to the processes laid out by the [Electoral Count Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Count_Act "Electoral Count Act") of 1887, [certificates of ascertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certificate_of_ascertainment "Certificate of ascertainment") listing the names of the electors and separate certificates recording their votes are distributed to various officials across the branches of government.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-37)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-38)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-39) The newly elected Congress, with the vice president in his role as Senate president presiding, met in a [joint session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_session_of_the_United_States_Congress "Joint session of the United States Congress") to formally open the certificates and count the votes, which began on January 6, 2021, was interrupted by the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), and finished the following day.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-40)

### Democratic Party

Main articles: [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"), [2020 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "2020 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection"), [2020 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_National_Convention "2020 Democratic National Convention"), and [Joe Biden 2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign "Joe Biden 2020 presidential campaign")

The Democratic Party chose its nominee in the [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"). [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") became the [presumptive nominee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumptive_nominee_(United_States) "Presumptive nominee (United States)") of the Democratic Party on April 8, 2020, after senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") of [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont") withdrew from the race.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-41) On June 5, 2020, Biden secured enough delegates to ensure his nomination at the national convention.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-42) Biden picked [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") as his vice-presidential nominee, and the ticket was formally nominated at the convention on August 18.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-43)

[Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election "United States presidential election") were held in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on November 3, 2020.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-ElectionDay-1) The [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") ticket of former [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States")[Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") junior [senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")[Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") defeated the incumbent [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")[president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and vice president [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-12) The election saw the highest [voter turnout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_turnout_in_United_States_presidential_elections "Voter turnout in United States presidential elections") by percentage [since 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_United_States_presidential_election "1900 United States presidential election"). Biden received more than 81 million votes,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-:7-13) the [most votes ever cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_candidates_by_number_of_votes_received "List of United States presidential candidates by number of votes received") for a presidential candidate in U.S. history.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-:8-14)

In a competitive primary that featured the most candidates for any political party in the [modern era of American politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Party_System "Sixth Party System"), Biden secured the [Democratic presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"). Biden's running mate, Harris, became the first African American, first Asian American, and third female[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-15) vice presidential nominee on a major party ticket. Trump easily secured re-nomination with only minor opposition in the [Republican primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Republican Party presidential primaries"). [Jo Jorgensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Jorgensen "Jo Jorgensen") secured the [Libertarian presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Libertarian_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Libertarian Party presidential primaries") with [Spike Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Cohen "Spike Cohen") as her running mate, and [Howie Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howie_Hawkins "Howie Hawkins") secured the [Green presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Green_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Green Party presidential primaries") with [Angela Nicole Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Nicole_Walker "Angela Nicole Walker") as his running mate.

The central issues of the election included the public health and [economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), [civil unrest in reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests "George Floyd protests") to the police [murder of George Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd"), the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") following the [death of Ruth Bader Ginsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg "Death and state funeral of Ruth Bader Ginsburg") and [confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Coney_Barrett_Supreme_Court_nomination "Amy Coney Barrett Supreme Court nomination"), and the future of the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-16) Due to the ongoing pandemic, a record number of ballots were [cast early](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_voting "Early voting") and [by mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting "Postal voting").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-:9-17) Thirty-eight states had over half of all votes cast using these methods, and only three states had fewer than 25%.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-18) As a result of a large number of mail-in ballots, some [swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state") saw delays in vote counting and reporting; this led to major news outlets delaying their projection of Biden and Harris as the [president-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_transition_of_Joe_Biden "Presidential transition of Joe Biden") and [vice president-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president-elect_of_the_United_States "Vice president-elect of the United States") until the morning of November 7, 2020.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-math-19)

Biden defeated Trump, winning 306 [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College") votes and 51.3% of the popular vote to Trump's 232 electoral votes and 46.8% of the popular vote. Trump was the first president to lose re-election since [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election"). Key to Biden's pivotal victory were his wins in the Democratic-leaning [Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt "Rust Belt") states of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Michigan "2020 United States presidential election in Michigan"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2020 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania"), and [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election_in_Wisconsin "2020 United States presidential election in Wisconsin"), which Trump narrowly carried in 2016 and whose combined 46 electoral votes were enough to swing the election to either candidate. This election marked the first time since [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_United_States_presidential_election "1948 United States presidential election") that the Democratic candidate won the popular vote in four consecutive elections.

Trump refused to accept the results; he and his allies made disproven claims of fraud, pressured election officials, filed several unsuccessful lawsuits,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-20)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-21)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-22) and directly [attempted to overturn the results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election "Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election") at the county, state, and federal level. This culminated in an [attack on the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack") on January 6, 2021, for which [Trump was impeached a second time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump "Second impeachment of Donald Trump"). The day after the attack, Trump stated that a "new administration" would be succeeding his, without mentioning president-elect Biden by name, in a video posted on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-23)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-24)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-25)

## Background

Further information: [United States presidential election §Procedure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election#Procedure "United States presidential election")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Donald_Trump_official_portrait.jpg/250px-Donald_Trump_official_portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_official_portrait.jpg)

[Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), the incumbent president in 2020, whose first non-consecutive term expired at noon on January 20, 2021

The [Maine Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Legislature "Maine Legislature") passed a bill in August 2019 adopting [ranked-choice voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranked-choice_voting_in_the_United_States "Ranked-choice voting in the United States") (RCV) both for presidential primaries and for the general election.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-ovz9x-26)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-qhJpi-27) Governor [Janet Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Mills "Janet Mills") allowed the bill to become law without her signature, which delayed its taking effect until after the [2020 Democratic primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Maine_Democratic_primary "2020 Maine Democratic primary") in March and made Maine the first state to use RCV for a presidential general election. The [Maine Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Republican_Party "Maine Republican Party") filed signatures for a [veto referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veto_referendum "Veto referendum") to preclude the use of RCV for the 2020 election, but [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Secretary_of_State "Maine Secretary of State")[Matthew Dunlap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Dunlap "Matthew Dunlap") found there were insufficient valid signatures to qualify for the ballot. A challenge in [Maine Superior Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Superior_Court "Maine Superior Court") was successful for the Maine Republican Party, but the [Maine Supreme Judicial Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Supreme_Judicial_Court "Maine Supreme Judicial Court")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-28)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-29) stayed the ruling pending appeal on September 8, 2020.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-30) Nevertheless, ballots began being printed later that day without the veto referendum and including RCV for the presidential election,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-31)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-forbes-32) and the Court ruled in favor of the secretary of state on September 22, allowing RCV to be used.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-33) An emergency appeal to the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") was denied on October 6.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-34) The law continues the use of the [congressional district method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_district_method "Congressional district method") for the allocation of Maine's electors ([Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") is the only other state that apportions its electoral votes this way).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-FcJYG-35) While multiple rounds of vote counting were not needed due to a single candidate receiving a majority of first-choice votes statewide and in each district, use of RCV complicates interpretation of the national [popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_election "Direct election") because voters are more likely to vote for third-party or independent candidates.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-36)

On December 14, 2020, pledged electors for each candidate, known collectively as the [United States Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), gathered in their states' capitols to cast their official votes. Pursuant to the processes laid out by the [Electoral Count Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Count_Act "Electoral Count Act") of 1887, [certificates of ascertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certificate_of_ascertainment "Certificate of ascertainment") listing the names of the electors and separate certificates recording their votes are distributed to various officials across the branches of government.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-37)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-38)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-39) The newly elected Congress, with the vice president in his role as Senate president presiding, met in a [joint session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_session_of_the_United_States_Congress "Joint session of the United States Congress") to formally open the certificates and count the votes, which began on January 6, 2021, was interrupted by the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), and finished the following day.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-40)

### Democratic Party

Main articles: [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"), [2020 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "2020 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection"), [2020 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_National_Convention "2020 Democratic National Convention"), and [Joe Biden 2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign "Joe Biden 2020 presidential campaign")

The Democratic Party chose its nominee in the [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"). [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") became the [presumptive nominee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumptive_nominee_(United_States) "Presumptive nominee (United States)") of the Democratic Party on April 8, 2020, after senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") of [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont") withdrew from the race.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-41) On June 5, 2020, Biden secured enough delegates to ensure his nomination at the national convention.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-42) Biden picked [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") as his vice-presidential nominee, and the ticket was formally nominated at the convention on August 18.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-43)

The trial in the Senate began on January 21, 2020, and ended on February 5, resulting in [[Acquittal#United States|acquittal]] by the [[United States Senate]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/02/05/trump-impeachment-vote-110805|title=Trump acquitted on impeachment charges, ending gravest threat to his presidency|first1=Kyle|last1=Cheney|first2=Andrew|last2=Desiderio|first3=John|last3=Bresnahan|date=February 5, 2020|access-date=February 5, 2020|work=[[Politico]]|archive-date=June 17, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200617023326/https://www.politico.com/news/2020/02/05/trump-impeachment-vote-110805|url-status=live}} This is the [[1868 Democratic National Convention|second]] time a president has been impeached during his first term while running for a second term.{{Cite web|url=https://www.historycentral.com/elections/Conventions/1868DEM.html|title=1868 Democratic Convention|website=History Central|access-date=November 8, 2020|archive-date=October 8, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008115442/https://www.historycentral.com/elections/Conventions/1868DEM.html|url-status=live}}{{efn|[[Andrew Johnson]] received votes during the [[1868 Democratic National Convention]], four months after having been [[Impeachment of Andrew Johnson|impeached]].{{Cite web|url=https://millercenter.org/president/johnson/campaigns-and-elections|title=Andrew Johnson: Campaigns and Elections|work=Miller Center|publisher=University of Virginia|last1=Varon|first1=Elizabeth R.|year=2019|access-date=November 1, 2020|archive-date=September 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200903114824/https://millercenter.org/president/johnson/campaigns-and-elections|url-status=live}}}} Trump continued to hold campaign rallies during the impeachment. This is also the first time since the modern presidential primaries were established in 1911 that a president has been subjected to impeachment while the primary season was underway. ELECTION RESULTS FOR THE U.S. PRESIDENT, THE U.S. SENATE
AND THE U.S. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

This publication has been prepared by the Federal Election Commission to provide the public with
the results of elections held in the fifty states during 2020 for the offices of United States President,
United States Senator and United States Representative.  Also included are the results for Delegate
to Congress from American Samoa, the District of Columbia, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands,
the U.S. Virgin Islands and Resident Commissioner for Puerto Rico.  Additionally, there are results
for the 2020 special elections to fill the unexpired U.S. Senate terms in Arizona and Georgia.  There
was one Congressional district seat left vacant after the 2020 general election, LA/05, due to the
December 2020 death of Representative-elect Luke J. Letlow.  Special election results for LA/05
and other special elections are included in Appendix 2.

In addition to the general election results, this publication includes the official results of the federal
primary and runoff elections.  As in the case of the general elections, primary elections are not
administered by the federal government.  In some states (such as Connecticut, Utah, and Virginia),
political party organizations control their nomination process by way of conventions.  In other
states, state law may regulate the primary and/or its administration.

The elections for these federal offices are administered by local election officials in towns, counties,
municipalities, and other jurisdictions.  The results of the elections are certified by the state
government, which in most cases is the Secretary of State.  While the full records are available for
public inspection, most states prepare summary reports for public dissemination.  These summary
reports vary in form and content, and may be amended well after the election.  There is no standard
format that states use in reporting federal election results.

Recognizing a need to bring together in one place the federal election results, the Commission
presents this publication as the 20th in a series designed to provide an accurate, historical record of
federal election results.  The Commission undertakes this project on a biennial basis in order to
respond to public inquiries, and as a research tool for Commission staff.

Data is based on official figures obtained from State election officials.  The Electoral Vote was
obtained from the State Certificates of Vote on file with the U.S. National Archives and Records
Administration.  If the election results are modified in the future, the Commission will supply errata
supplements as necessary.  The assistance provided by the State election officials and their staff in
the preparation of this publication is greatly appreciated.

Federal Elections 2020 may also be viewed and/or downloaded from the Commission’s website,
https://www.fec.gov.

EXPLANATORY NOTES

•  The candidate who was the winner of the general election is listed first in the entry for each state
and district (where applicable).  After that, the candidates are arranged by party affiliation.

•  Incumbent Congressional candidates facing re-election in 2020 are designated with an (I) to the
left of the candidate’s name.  The lack of an (I) in a particular Senate race or U.S. House district
indicates an open seat race.

•  The party affiliation of the candidate is as listed on the ballot and has been abbreviated.  A
complete listing of party abbreviations appears at the end of this publication.

•  Totals for write-in votes are shown as disclosed by the state.  Some states list the names of
candidates who received write-in votes, while others provide a write-in vote total without the
names of the candidates who received the votes.  Still other states combine these two variations
and provide the names of some candidates who received write-in votes and a total of write-in
votes for all the other candidates.  Registered write-in candidates that received “0” votes are not
included.

•  In some states, there were unopposed candidates whose names did not appear on a ballot and
therefore received no votes.

•  “Total Votes,” “Total State Votes,” “Party Votes,” and “District Votes” represent all the valid
votes cast for the candidates in the election.  State totals (and the totals for the territories and the
District of Columbia) are found in the summary charts and at the end of each state/territory
section.  Blank, void, under and over votes are not included.

•  “Combined Parties” represents all the valid votes cast for one candidate, regardless of party.
(This method is used where a candidate may be listed on the ballot more than once, with
different party designations, i.e., Connecticut and New York.)  These votes are then broken down
and listed by party.  The party votes are enclosed by brackets [ ].

•  The percentage of votes received by each general election candidate is based on the figure of
total votes.  The percentage of votes received by each candidate in a primary or runoff election is
based on the figure of total votes cast in that specific primary or runoff election.

•  Due to the rounding of percentage numbers, some percentages may not total 100%.  Also, some
states differ in how they round percentages.  The percentages in this publication were all rounded
the same way and may not match the percentages as reported by the state.

ELECTION RESULTS FOR THE U.S. PRESIDENT, THE U.S. SENATE
AND THE U.S. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

This publication has been prepared by the Federal Election Commission to provide the public with
the results of elections held in the fifty states during 2020 for the offices of United States President,
United States Senator and United States Representative.  Also included are the results for Delegate
to Congress from American Samoa, the District of Columbia, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands,
the U.S. Virgin Islands and Resident Commissioner for Puerto Rico.  Additionally, there are results
for the 2020 special elections to fill the unexpired U.S. Senate terms in Arizona and Georgia.  There
was one Congressional district seat left vacant after the 2020 general election, LA/05, due to the
December 2020 death of Representative-elect Luke J. Letlow.  Special election results for LA/05
and other special elections are included in Appendix 2.

In addition to the general election results, this publication includes the official results of the federal
primary and runoff elections.  As in the case of the general elections, primary elections are not
administered by the federal government.  In some states (such as Connecticut, Utah, and Virginia),
political party organizations control their nomination process by way of conventions.  In other
states, state law may regulate the primary and/or its administration.

The elections for these federal offices are administered by local election officials in towns, counties,
municipalities, and other jurisdictions.  The results of the elections are certified by the state
government, which in most cases is the Secretary of State.  While the full records are available for
public inspection, most states prepare summary reports for public dissemination.  These summary
reports vary in form and content, and may be amended well after the election.  There is no standard
format that states use in reporting federal election results.

Recognizing a need to bring together in one place the federal election results, the Commission
presents this publication as the 20th in a series designed to provide an accurate, historical record of
federal election results.  The Commission undertakes this project on a biennial basis in order to
respond to public inquiries, and as a research tool for Commission staff.

Data is based on official figures obtained from State election officials.  The Electoral Vote was
obtained from the State Certificates of Vote on file with the U.S. National Archives and Records
Administration.  If the election results are modified in the future, the Commission will supply errata
supplements as necessary.  The assistance provided by the State election officials and their staff in
the preparation of this publication is greatly appreciated.

Federal Elections 2020 may also be viewed and/or downloaded from the Commission’s website,
https://www.fec.gov.

EXPLANATORY NOTES

•  The candidate who was the winner of the general election is listed first in the entry for each state
and district (where applicable).  After that, the candidates are arranged by party affiliation.

•  Incumbent Congressional candidates facing re-election in 2020 are designated with an (I) to the
left of the candidate’s name.  The lack of an (I) in a particular Senate race or U.S. House district
indicates an open seat race.

•  The party affiliation of the candidate is as listed on the ballot and has been abbreviated.  A
complete listing of party abbreviations appears at the end of this publication.

•  Totals for write-in votes are shown as disclosed by the state.  Some states list the names of
candidates who received write-in votes, while others provide a write-in vote total without the
names of the candidates who received the votes.  Still other states combine these two variations
and provide the names of some candidates who received write-in votes and a total of write-in
votes for all the other candidates.  Registered write-in candidates that received “0” votes are not
included.

•  In some states, there were unopposed candidates whose names did not appear on a ballot and
therefore received no votes.

•  “Total Votes,” “Total State Votes,” “Party Votes,” and “District Votes” represent all the valid
votes cast for the candidates in the election.  State totals (and the totals for the territories and the
District of Columbia) are found in the summary charts and at the end of each state/territory
section.  Blank, void, under and over votes are not included.

•  “Combined Parties” represents all the valid votes cast for one candidate, regardless of party.
(This method is used where a candidate may be listed on the ballot more than once, with
different party designations, i.e., Connecticut and New York.)  These votes are then broken down
and listed by party.  The party votes are enclosed by brackets [ ].

•  The percentage of votes received by each general election candidate is based on the figure of
total votes.  The percentage of votes received by each candidate in a primary or runoff election is
based on the figure of total votes cast in that specific primary or runoff election.

•  Due to the rounding of percentage numbers, some percentages may not total 100%.  Also, some
states differ in how they round percentages.  The percentages in this publication were all rounded
the same way and may not match the percentages as reported by the state.

## Sources

Although adjusted for variations in age distribution and population size, differences by state do not account for other state-specific population characteristics that may affect death rates.

When the number of deaths is small, differences between states and rankings by state may be unreliable due to instability in rates.
